extracted.intended_audience: empirical legal scholars, patent scholars, patent litigators, and policymakers researching patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for locating, selecting, and hand-coding federal district-court patent lawsuits (2008–2009) to produce an empirical data set of litigation outcomes by patent and claim. Covers inclusion/exclusion rules, unit of analysis, coding granularity, sources, reliability checks, and classification of technologies and industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset time window and case selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Study covers all patent lawsuits filed in federal district courts between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2009.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selected years because they are sufficiently recent to snapshot current litigation and because most cases filed in those years were resolved before coding (only ~2–3% still open as of Feb 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criterion — types of actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Include lawsuits that include a complaint alleging infringement of a utility patent or seeking declaratory relief of noninfringement or invalidity of a utility patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude licensing disputes, malpractice actions, and allegations of design or plant patent infringement. Focus is on utility-patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data source requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Lex Machina as the primary data source, which provides cleaned and verified PACER data for district-court patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: Lex Machina includes all lawsuits (even those without a decision on Westlaw/Lexis), cleans many PACER errors, and indexes summary judgment rulings, trial events, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual docket review and document reading
rubrics_metrics.description: For each case, read all relevant orders, opinions, motions, verdicts, appellate rulings, and other necessary court documents to code litigation outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an opinion lacks sufficient detail to ascertain the basis for a ruling, read the underlying briefing by the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis — patent-case combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of analysis is a patent-case combination; outcome coded separately for each asserted patent in a civil action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple civil actions involve the same patent, code them as separate observations (even if consolidated). If different claims within a patent have different substantive outcomes, create a new record for each group of claims with a different outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of consolidated lawsuits in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: While descriptive statistics include each patent in each civil action (including consolidated lawsuits), regression models account for consolidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cluster standard errors at both the patent and case level in regression models to account for consolidated lawsuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of rulings to capture — merits decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture all rulings on summary judgment relating to patent-law issues and all trial outcomes, whether jury or bench, and post-verdict JMOL decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes rulings on motions of summary judgment on noninfringement, invalidity, no inequitable conduct, and inequitable conduct. Exclude rulings that are not patent-specific (e.g., laches) and summary judgment rulings where the court did not reach the merits (e.g., premature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include appeals and appellate resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Record whether an appeal was lodged and how the appeal was resolved (affirmed, reversed, pending, dismissed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Federal Circuit reverses a ruling on appeal, update the final-resolution coding to reflect the appellate decision; retain the original trial-court summary judgment coding to capture trial-court win rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final vs interim resolution coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions that finally rule for a party on an issue are coded as definitive wins; decisions that rule for a party but keep the issue alive (largely denials of summary judgment and remands) are coded as interim wins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant of summary judgment is coded as a final resolution on that issue; denial alone is not a final resolution because it leaves a disputed issue of material fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity of invalidity coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Code invalidity rulings at a low level of granularity: utility, patentable subject matter, § 102 prior art, obviousness (§ 103), indefiniteness (§ 112), written description, enablement, and best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also code various bases for § 102 invalidity (different grounds under prior art). Include merits rulings on each issue even if the ruling was not the final resolution (subject to the 'moot' exclusion rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity of infringement and unenforceability coding
rubrics_metrics.description: For infringement code literal infringement and the doctrine of equivalents; for unenforceability code types of unenforceability and their bases (e.g., inequitable conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture direct (literal + DOE) and various indirect infringement types as litigated to decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of merits rulings regardless of stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Code issues litigated to decision whether or not that decision resulted in a trial outcome or a grant of summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if a court denies two invalidity arguments but grants a third, include all three rulings in the data set (except those denied as moot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of moot motion rulings
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include an issue in the data set if the court denied the motion as moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the court grants summary judgment on one issue and denies another as moot, include the granted issue but not the moot-denied issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding of issue-level vs claim-level outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the court rules differently on different claims of a patent (e.g., one claim infringed and another not), create separate records at the claim or claim-group level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can reduce the unit from patent to individual claim or group-of-claims when outcomes diverge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coder qualifications and hands-on coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Because patent dockets are complex, experienced patent litigators (Mark Lemley and David Schwartz) personally coded approximately half the lawsuits each rather than using student coders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coding requires deep knowledge of patent law and litigation and significant time; the authors spent several hundred hours on hand coding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercoder overlap and codebook refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate reliability, the authors overlapped their coding: initially ~5% each, then overlapped ~10% of cases, and then an additional random 15% overlap; they compared results and fine-tuned the codebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revisit overlapping dockets to resolve disagreements and correct the data set accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercoder reliability measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Cohen’s kappa (κ) to measure intercoder reliability for coding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported κ values: 0.9534 for basic definitive and interim winners; 0.9793 for grants of motions for summary judgment on invalidity and noninfringement—interpreted as near-perfect agreement. Investigate and correct identified discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling complexity and undercount risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that complexity of dockets may lead to slight undercounting of merits rulings and that some motions may be missed despite high κ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revisit dockets for disagreements; correct known disagreements; recognize that undercounting may not be biased in a particular direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture of patent demographic and case covariates
rubrics_metrics.description: For each patent in a lawsuit, obtain patent demographic information (e.g., adjusted number of citations received, total prior art references, number of claims, age of patent at litigation filing) and facts about the lawsuit (e.g., number of defendants, number of asserted patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These covariates are used in descriptive statistics and regression models and are important controls when comparing outcomes across technologies and industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology vs industry classification principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate 'technology' categories (nature of the invention) from 'industry' categories (owner of the patents and the industry in which the technology is put to use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some terms (e.g., 'biotechnology') may be used for both technology and industry but must be disambiguated; e.g., patents on gene sequences used in gene therapy might be both tech and industry depending on application. PTO classes are not treated as authoritative for defining technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of cases with appeals but without summary-judgment/trial list
rubrics_metrics.description: Include cases provided by Lex Machina that had appeals but without a summary judgment ruling or trial to capture cases where parties stipulated to judgment post claim construction to preserve appealability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a second Lex Machina list to capture these stipulation/appeal-focused cases and ensure they are reviewed and coded as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of appellate reversal in summary-judgment coding
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain the original trial-court summary judgment coding for trial-court win rates but update final-resolution coding to reflect appellate reversals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not eliminate trial-court summary-judgment observations even if later reversed, because capturing trial-court behavior is an explicit study goal; final-resolution variables reflect appellate outcomes when applicable.
